reference.source: Williams Obstetrics / Novak's Gynecology / Campbell-Walsh Urology
clinicalPearls: Undescended testis (cryptorchidism) is failure of one or both testes to reach the scrotum, and is among the commonest congenital genitourinary anomalies in boys, more frequent in preterm infants
Many testes that are undescended at birth descend spontaneously within the first few months, so definitive management is guided by examination after this early window
It is important to distinguish a true undescended testis from a retractile testis, which can be manipulated into the scrotum and stays there, and requires observation rather than surgery
A truly impalpable testis raises the possibility of an intra-abdominal, absent, or atrophic (vanished) testis and warrants surgical evaluation
Bilateral non-palpable testes, especially with hypospadias or other genital ambiguity, should prompt urgent evaluation for a disorder of sex development
Imaging is unreliable for locating an impalpable testis, and laparoscopy is the definitive means of identifying and managing it
Orchidopexy, ideally performed in early childhood, brings the testis into the scrotum to optimise fertility potential, allow examination, and reduce though not eliminate cancer risk
Cryptorchidism is associated with reduced fertility and an increased lifetime risk of testicular germ cell tumour, in both the affected and, to a lesser degree, the contralateral testis
An acutely painful, swollen groin or scrotum in a boy with an undescended testis should raise concern for torsion of that testis
reference.pathophysiology: Testicular descent occurs in two phases governed by hormonal and mechanical factors: a transabdominal phase dependent on insulin-like factor 3 and the gubernaculum, and an inguinoscrotal phase dependent on androgens and the genitofemoral nerve. Disruption of these hormonal signals, gubernacular development, or the mechanical pathway leaves the testis arrested anywhere along its normal route from the abdomen to the scrotum, or in an ectopic position. The undescended testis is exposed to a higher-than-scrotal temperature, which impairs germ cell maturation over time, accounting for reduced fertility, and it carries intrinsic and environmental factors that raise malignancy risk.
additionalDifferentials: Ectopic testis (outside the normal line of descent)
Disorder of sex development in bilateral impalpable cases
Inguinal hernia presenting as a groin swelling
additionalInvestigations: Careful repeated clinical examination in a warm, relaxed setting to determine palpability and position
Laparoscopy as the definitive investigation for an impalpable testis
Hormonal evaluation (including gonadotrophins and testosterone-axis testing) in bilateral impalpable cases
Karyotype and endocrine work-up where a disorder of sex development is suspected
Ultrasound has limited value and should not delay surgical referral for an impalpable testis
redFlags: Bilateral impalpable testes, particularly with hypospadias, suggesting a disorder of sex development requiring urgent assessment
Acute pain and swelling in an undescended or inguinal testis suggesting torsion
A previously descended testis that has ascended (acquired cryptorchidism)
A firm or enlarging testicular mass raising concern for malignancy in later life
Associated genital ambiguity or endocrine abnormality
reference.prognosis: Timely orchidopexy in early childhood improves fertility outcomes, particularly in unilateral cases, and facilitates self-examination and earlier tumour detection. Bilateral disease carries greater fertility risk. The increased risk of testicular cancer persists into adulthood despite surgery, so lifelong awareness and self-examination are advised. Retractile testes generally have a benign course but need follow-up because a minority ascend.
pitfalls: Confusing a retractile testis with a true undescended testis and operating unnecessarily
Relying on ultrasound to locate an impalpable testis and delaying definitive laparoscopy
Missing a disorder of sex development in bilateral impalpable testes with genital anomalies
Deferring orchidopexy beyond the optimal early window, compromising fertility potential
Reassuring families that surgery abolishes the future cancer risk
